docs.text: AsyncMonolith AsyncMonolith is a lightweight library that facilitates simple, durable and asynchronous messaging in dotnet apps. Overview: Speed up your API by offloading tasks to a background worker. Distribute workload amongst multiple app instances. Execute tasks at specific times or after a delay. Execute tasks at regular intervals. Simplify complex processes by building out an event-driven architecture. Decouple your services by utilizing the Mediator pattern. Improve your application's resiliency by utilizing the Transactional Outbox pattern. Improve your application's resiliency by utilizing automatic retries. Keep your infrastructure simple without using a message broker. Simplify testability. [!NOTE] Despite its name, AsyncMonolith can be used within a microservices architecture. The only requirement is that the producers and consumers share the same database i.e messaging within a single project. However, it is not suitable for passing messages between different projects in a microservices architecture, as microservices should not share the same database. Note Despite its name, AsyncMonolith can be used within a microservices architecture. The only requirement is that the producers and consumers share the same database i.e messaging within a single project. However, it is not suitable for passing messages between different projects in a microservices architecture, as microservices should not share the same database. Support 🛟 Need help? docs.text: Hit https://localhost:60046/api/spam?count=1000 to see how performant AsyncMonolith is on your system. With 10 message batches and single processor instance I usually process (trivial) messages at <10ms each. The demo is setup to run against a PostgreSql database, make sure you've got docker installed

docs.text: ProducerService Resolves consumers for a given payload and writes messages to the consumer_messages table for processing. ScheduleService Writes scheduled messages to the scheduled_messages table. Tables ConfigureAsyncMonolith() maps three tables (with an optional schema and table prefix): consumer_messages : one row per pending message per consumer. scheduled_messages : recurring schedules and when they are next due. poisoned_messages : messages that failed every attempt, with the last error. ConsumerMessageProcessor One background processor runs per rail. Each cycle it: Claims a batch in a short transaction: it reads due messages (locking rows on PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL and MariaDB), then for each one counts the attempt and leases it by moving available_after past the consumer's timeout plus 30 seconds. The update only applies if the message is unchanged since it was read, so only one processor can claim it. Consumes each claimed message outside any transaction, in its own DI scope, so consumers can use the database freely. Completes each message in its own short write: deleted on success, otherwise retried after a backoff delay, or moved to poisoned_messages after its last attempt. If its lease was taken over meanwhile, nothing is changed. If the app stops mid-message, the message becomes available again when its lease expires. ScheduledMessageProcessor Reads due schedules and, for each one, moves it to its next occurrence (conditionally, so each occurrence fires once across instances) and produces a message for every consumer of its payload. A schedule that can't be evaluated is checked again an hour later without affecting the others. It also deletes expired poisoned messages when PoisonedMessageRetention is set. Notes 📋 After a batch that wasn't full a processor waits IdlePollInterval ; after a full batch it waits BusyPollInterval . While batches keep failing (for example during a database outage) the wait doubles up to 30 seconds. Consumers and payloads are found by scanning the registered assemblies at startup, and the registry is checked for name clashes and payloads without consumers when the host starts.

docs.text: For a more detailed example look at the Demo project Install the nuget package to support your database dotnet add package AsyncMonolith Setup your DbContext public class ApplicationDbContext : DbContext { public ApplicationDbContext ( DbContextOptions < ApplicationDbContext > options ) : base ( options ) { } // Map AsyncMonolith's tables. DbSet properties for them are optional. protected override void OnModelCreating ( ModelBuilder modelBuilder ) { modelBuilder . ConfigureAsyncMonolith (); // Or keep them apart from your own tables: // modelBuilder.ConfigureAsyncMonolith(o => // { // o.Schema = "jobs"; // databases that support schemas // o.TablePrefix = "jobs_"; // jobs_consumer_messages, ... // }); base . OnModelCreating ( modelBuilder ); } } If you're not using ef migrations check out the sql to configure your database here Register your dependencies and configure settings // Your DbContext, with any EF Core provider builder . Services . AddDbContext < ApplicationDbContext > ( o => o . UseNpgsql ( connectionString )); // AsyncMonolith picks its queries from the provider: PostgreSQL (Npgsql), SQL Server, and MySQL or MariaDB // (MySql.EntityFrameworkCore or Pomelo) lock rows so several app instances can share the tables. Any other // provider, such as SQLite, works without row locks (fine for a single instance). builder . Services . AddAsyncMonolith < ApplicationDbContext > ( options => { options . RegisterTypesFromAssemblyContaining < Program > (); options . MaxAttempts = 5 ; // Attempts before a message is poisoned options . AttemptDelay = TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 10 ); // First retry delay; doubles each retry options . MaxAttemptDelay = TimeSpan . FromMinutes ( 5 ); // Longest retry delay options . DefaultConsumerTimeout = TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 10 ); // Before a consumer is cancelled options . BatchSize = 5 ; // Messages a processor takes at once options . IdlePollInterval = TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 1 ); // Wait after a batch that wasn't full options . BusyPollInterval = TimeSpan . FromMilliseconds ( 10 ); // Wait after a full batch }) . BindConfiguration ( "AsyncMonolith" ); // Optional: override any option from appsettings.json Options are validated when the host starts, so an invalid value stops startup with an OptionsValidationException that names it. In appsettings.json , write times as "00:00:30" . The following methods are available on the AsyncMonolithOptions passed into the options lambda: RegisterTypesFromAssemblyContaining<T>() RegisterTypesFromAssemblyContaining(Type type) RegisterTypesFromAssembly(Assembly assembly) RegisterTypesFromAssemblies(params Assembly[] assemblies) Modules Call AddAsyncMonolith once, in the host. A module or library with its own consumers registers them itself, before or after the host's call: services . AddAsyncMonolithConsumersFromAssemblyContaining < BillingModule > (); // or services . AddAsyncMonolithConsumers ( typeof ( BillingModule ). Assembly ); Registering an assembly more than once is harmless. Consumers from every module are checked together when the host starts: a payload with no consumer in any module, or two payloads or consumers with the same stored name, stops startup with an error (see Stored names ). Create messages and consumers // Define Consumer Payload public class ValueSubmitted : IConsumerPayload { [JsonPropertyName("value")] public required double Value { get ; set ; } } // Define Consumer [ConsumerTimeout(5)] // Consumer timeouts after 5 seconds [ConsumerAttempts(1)] // Consumer messages moved to poisoned table after 1 failed attempt public class ValueSubmittedConsumer : IConsumer < ValueSubmitted > { private readonly ApplicationDbContext _dbContext ; private readonly IProducerService _producerService ; public ValueSubmittedConsumer ( ApplicationDbContext dbContext , IProducerService producerService ) { _dbContext = dbContext ; _producerService = producerService ; } public Task Consume ( ValueSubmitted message , ConsumeContext context , CancellationToken cancellationToken ) { ... await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken ); } } Produce / schedule messages // Inject services private readonly IProducerService _producerService ; private readonly IScheduleService _scheduleService ; // Produce a message to be processed immediately await _producerService . Produce ( new ValueSubmitted () { Value = newValue }); // Produce a message to be processed in 10 seconds await _producerService . Produce ( new ValueSubmitted () { Value = newValue }, 10 ); // Produce a message to be processed in 10 seconds, but only once for a given userId await _producerService . Produce ( new ValueSubmitted () { Value = newValue }, TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 10 ), $"user:{userId}" ); // Publish a message every Monday at 12pm (UTC) with a tag that can be used to modify / delete related scheduled messages. _scheduleService . Schedule ( new ValueSubmitted { Value = newValue }, "0 0 12 * * MON" , "UTC" , "id:{id}" ); // Save changes await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken );

docs.text: Make sure to check this table before updating the nuget package in your solution, you may be required to add an dotnet ef migration . Version Description Migration Required 11.0.0 One package, multi-instance-safe processing, new consumer and options APIs (see below) Yes 8.0.6 Added ConsumerAttempts override attribute No 8.0.5 Bundle debug symbols with nuget package No 8.0.4 Bundle XML docs with nuget package No 8.0.3 Optimised Sql No 8.0.2 Added distributed trace_id and span_id No 8.0.1 Added OpenTelemetry support Yes 8.0.0 Use Producer & Schedule service interfaces No 1.0.9 Initial Yes If you're not using ef migrations check out the sql to configure your database here 11.0.0 AsyncMonolith is now a single package. From 11.0.0 the major version follows Semantic Versioning (it changes for breaking changes) rather than the .NET version. It is tested against PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL 8.4 (with Oracle's MySql.EntityFrameworkCore ), MariaDB 11.8 and SQLite. Upgrading from 8.x or 10.x Replace AsyncMonolith.Ef , .PostgreSql , .MsSql , .MySql or .MariaDb with the AsyncMonolith package, and add your EF Core provider if your app doesn't reference it already. Replace services.Add{Database}AsyncMonolith<TDbContext>(settings => ...) with services.AddAsyncMonolith<TDbContext>(options => ...) , converting times to TimeSpan s (see the options changes below). Make consumers implement IConsumer<TPayload> and add the ConsumeContext context parameter to Consume . Call modelBuilder.ConfigureAsyncMonolith() in OnModelCreating , then add and apply a migration (see below). On PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL or MariaDB, make sure every Produce is followed by SaveChangesAsync : messages are no longer written without it. Migration required. Add a migration ( dotnet ef migrations add AsyncMonolith_11_0_0 ). It adds a nullable last_error column to consumer_messages and poisoned_messages . It also adds indexes for finding due messages ( rail_id, available_after ), due schedules ( available_after ), schedules by tag, and poisoned messages by age, which keep processing fast as the tables grow. If you manage the schema by hand, see the SQL schemas . They also now include rail_id , and their trace_id and span_id columns are nullable. Changes - Metrics on the async_monolith meter, and optional PoisonedMessageRetention . - A schedule that can't be evaluated, or whose payload has no consumers, no longer stops the others. A consumer that ignores cancellation is abandoned two seconds after its timeout. Processors back off while the database is unavailable. - Cron expressions can have 5 fields (minute precision) as well as 6 (seconds first). - AsyncMonolithOptions.SerializerOptions sets the JsonSerializerOptions for payloads. The default is unchanged. - Tables can live in their own schema or have a prefix: modelBuilder.ConfigureAsyncMonolith(o => { o.Schema = "jobs"; o.TablePrefix = "jobs_"; }) . The row-locking SQL follows the mapping. - Every database now produces messages the same way: they are added to your DbContext and written on SaveChanges , in your transaction. The PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL and MariaDB packages used to write immediately. A repeated deduplication key skips consumers that already have a pending message with it, on every database. - Several app instances can safely share the tables with any database. Claims and schedule occurrences use conditional updates, so a message is processed by one processor at a time and a schedule fires once per occurrence. - Fetch order is deterministic (oldest first, then by id). See Ordering for what is and isn't guaranteed. - Consumers can write to the database on SQLite. Messages are claimed and leased in a short transaction, consumers run outside it, and each message is completed in its own short write. If the app stops mid-message, the message is retried once its consumer timeout plus 30 seconds has passed. - Retries back off exponentially from AttemptDelay up to the new MaxAttemptDelay option (default 5 minutes). - The last error is stored on retried and poisoned messages. - IPoisonedMessageService counts, lists, retries and deletes poisoned messages. - IScheduleService.EnsureSchedule creates or updates a schedule by tag, so it can run at every startup. - IQueueStatisticsService reports queue depth and the age of the oldest due message, for health checks. - [ConsumerPayloadName] and [ConsumerName] give payloads and consumers stable stored names. Name clashes now fail at startup instead of silently mixing messages. - AddAsyncMonolithConsumers lets modules register their own consumers alongside the host's AddAsyncMonolith call. Breaking changes - One package. AsyncMonolith.Ef , .PostgreSql , .MsSql , .MySql and .MariaDb are replaced by AsyncMonolith alone, and AddEfAsyncMonolith / AddPostgreSqlAsyncMonolith /... by AddAsyncMonolith<TDbContext>() . The queries are chosen from your DbContext's EF Core provider, and AsyncMonolith no longer references any database driver: bring your own provider (for MySQL, MySql.EntityFrameworkCore ; Pomelo works once it supports EF Core 10). - ConfigureAsyncMonolith() now maps all three tables (previously only an index), so DbSet properties for them are optional. It takes an optional schema and table prefix. The [Table] attributes on the entities are removed; call ConfigureAsyncMonolith() in OnModelCreating if you weren't already. - IPoisonedMessageService.List returns PoisonedMessageInfo records with DateTimeOffset times instead of PoisonedMessage entities. - Implementation types are now internal: ConsumerRegistry , the processors and processor factory, the fetchers and their interfaces, ScheduleService , PoisonedMessageService , QueueStatisticsService , AsyncMonolithIdGenerator , AsyncMonolithInstrumentation.ActivitySource (the source name constants stay public), and ScheduledMessage.GetNextOccurrence / UpdateSchedule / UpdatePayload . Use the service interfaces instead. FakeProducerService is created by AddFakeAsyncMonolithBaseServices . - IProducerService.Produce takes a TimeSpan? delay or a DateTimeOffset availableAt instead of a Unix-seconds long availableAfter , and insertId is renamed deduplicationKey (still stored in insert_id ). ProduceList takes an IEnumerable<T> . Produce(ScheduledMessage) is no longer on the interface. - Renamed: ChronExpression / ChronTimezone → CronExpression / CronTimeZone (columns unchanged), InsertId → DeduplicationKey (column unchanged), ConsumerInstanceExecutionMode → ConsumerExecutionMode , and IScheduleService parameters to cronExpression / timeZone . No migration is needed for these. - AsyncMonolithSettings is now AsyncMonolithOptions , configured through the standard options pattern and validated when the host starts (an OptionsValidationException instead of an ArgumentException at registration). Times are TimeSpan s, and some names changed: ProcessorBatchSize → BatchSize , ProcessorMaxDelay (ms) → IdlePollInterval , ProcessorMinDelay (ms) → BusyPollInterval . AsyncMonolithSettings.Default is gone; use new AsyncMonolithOptions() . - AddAsyncMonolith returns an AsyncMonolithBuilder (for .BindConfiguration(...) and .AddConsumers(...) ) instead of IServiceCollection , and the obsolete overloads taking an Assembly are removed. The TestHelpers setup methods take Action<AsyncMonolithOptions> . - [ConsumerTimeout] 's Duration property is now Seconds . - Consumers implement IConsumer<TPayload> and receive a ConsumeContext ; BaseConsumer<T> is removed. - PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL and MariaDB users: messages are no longer written until you call SaveChanges . If you produced messages without saving, call SaveChangesAsync . - AddAsyncMonolith no longer registers DbContext as an alias for your context, and throws if called twice (modules use AddAsyncMonolithConsumers ). Its services use TryAdd , so services you register first win. - Removed public types: the per-database producer services and the unused ScheduledMessageProcessorFactory . Resolve IProducerService instead. - AsyncMonolith.TestHelpers uses xunit v3, and ConsumerTestBase.InitializeAsync / DisposeAsync return ValueTask . - IScheduleService has a new member ( EnsureSchedule ), so custom implementations must add it. - Errors that were thrown as System.Exception are now InvalidOperationException . - TestConsumerMessageProcessor.ProcessNext<TDbContext, TConsumer> now finds the consumer's message. It previously always returned null.

docs.text: AsyncMonolith.Tests Tests are split into two groups: Fast tests run in-process with no external services. Run them on every change: dotnet test --project AsyncMonolith.Tests --filter-not-trait "Category=Integration" Integration tests ( [Trait("Category", "Integration")] ) use Testcontainers to run against real databases, so they need Docker and are much slower. Run them before a release: dotnet test --project AsyncMonolith.Tests --filter-trait "Category=Integration" On Apple Silicon, SQL Server runs under emulation and needs about 2 GB per container. If SQL Server containers exit with code 114, give Docker more memory or run the tests one class at a time with --parallel none (about 9 minutes for the whole suite). Add --coverage --coverage-output-format cobertura to either command for a coverage report. CI uploads one for each run as an artifact. AsyncMonolith.TestHelpers Install the TestHelpers package to help with unit / integration tests. It targets xunit v3 ( xunit.v3 ). FakeIdGenerator Generates sequential fake id's of the format $"fake-id-{invocationCount}" ConsumerMessageTestHelpers Static methods for asserting messages have been inserted into the consumer_messages table. FakeProducerService Provides a fake IProducerService implementation, which is useful for asserting messages have been published without using a database. FakeScheduleService Provides a fake IScheduleService implementation, which is useful for asserting messages have been scheduled without using a database. SetupTestHelpers Includes two methods to configure your IServiceCollection without including the background services for processing messages. AddFakeAsyncMonolithBaseServices configures fake services which don't depend on a database AddRealAsyncMonolithBaseServices configures real services without registering the background processors TestConsumerMessageProcessor Static methods for invoking and testing your consumers. ConsumerTestBase The ConsumerTestBase offers a way to write simple tests for your consumers public class CancelShipmentTests : ConsumerTestBase { public CancelShipmentTests ( ITestOutputHelper testOutputHelper ) : base ( testOutputHelper ) { } private readonly string _inMemoryDatabaseName = Guid . docs.text: Tests are split into two groups: Fast tests run in-process with no external services. Run them on every change: dotnet test --project AsyncMonolith.Tests --filter-not-trait "Category=Integration" Integration tests ( [Trait("Category", "Integration")] ) use Testcontainers to run against real databases, so they need Docker and are much slower. Run them before a release: dotnet test --project AsyncMonolith.Tests --filter-trait "Category=Integration" On Apple Silicon, SQL Server runs under emulation and needs about 2 GB per container. If SQL Server containers exit with code 114, give Docker more memory or run the tests one class at a time with --parallel none (about 9 minutes for the whole suite). Add --coverage --coverage-output-format cobertura to either command for a coverage report. CI uploads one for each run as an artifact.

docs.text: Row locking depends on your database. With PostgreSQL (Npgsql), SQL Server, and MySQL or MariaDB (MySql.EntityFrameworkCore or Pomelo), processors lock rows and skip each other's batches. With any other EF Core provider, such as SQLite, several app instances read the same candidate messages and compete for them. Claims are conditional, so a message is still processed by only one instance, but instances waste work. That is fine for a single instance. Consumers run at least once. A message can run again if the app stops mid-message, or if a consumer ignores its cancellation token and is abandoned. Make consumers idempotent: ConsumeContext.MessageId and ConsumeContext.DeduplicationKey help. Honour the CancellationToken . It is cancelled at the consumer's timeout and when the app stops. Batches finish together. A processor waits for every consumer in its batch before taking the next, so a slow consumer delays the others on its rail. Put slow consumers on their own rail with [ConsumerRailId] , or raise their [ConsumerTimeout] . No ordering guarantee. See Ordering . Test your expected throughput against your database before relying on it.
docs.title: Warnings ⚠️

docs.text: Backwards Compatibility : When modifying consumer payload schemas, ensure changes are backwards compatible so that existing messages with the old schema can still be processed. Schema Migration : If changes are not backwards compatible, make the changes in a copy of the ConsumerPayload (with a different class name) and update all consumers to operate on the new payload. Once all messages with the old payload schema have been processed, you can safely delete the old payload schema and its associated consumers. Stored names Messages are stored with the name of their payload type ( payload_type ) and consumer type ( consumer_type ). By default that is the class name, so renaming a payload or consumer class breaks messages and schedules that are already stored . Give a type a stable name to decouple it from the class name: [ConsumerPayloadName("minicms.email.send")] public class SendEmail : IConsumerPayload { ... } [ConsumerName("minicms.email.sender")] public class SendEmailConsumer : IConsumer < SendEmail > { ... } To rename a class that already has stored messages, add the attribute with the old class name first. Names must be unique across everything registered. Two payloads or consumers with the same stored name, such as SendEmail classes in two modules, fail at startup with an error naming both types.

docs.text: Independent Consumption : Each message will be consumed independently by each consumer set up to handle it. Periodic Querying : Each instance of your app will periodically query the consumer_messages table for a batch of available messages to process. After a batch that wasn't full it waits IdlePollInterval before looking again; after a full batch it waits BusyPollInterval . Multiple instances : Any number of app instances can process the same tables, with any database. A processor claims each message with a conditional update, so a message is only ever claimed by one processor at a time, and each schedule occurrence fires once. On PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL and MariaDB, processors also lock rows while claiming, so processors skip each other's batches instead of competing for them. Rails : Each rail ( [ConsumerRailId] ) gets its own processor, so a slow consumer on one rail doesn't hold up consumers on another. Batching : Consumer messages will be read from the consumer_messages table in batches defined by BatchSize . Idempotency : Ensure your Consumers are idempotent, since they will be retried on failure. Timeout : Consumers timeout after the number of seconds defined by the ConsumerTimeout attribute or the DefaultConsumerTimeout if not set. Pass the CancellationToken to everything your consumer awaits. A consumer that ignores it is abandoned two seconds after its timeout so its rail can carry on, but it may keep running in the background while the message is retried. Consumers implement IConsumer<TPayload> . The ConsumeContext describes the message and this attempt: MessageId , DeduplicationKey , Attempt (starting at 1), MaxAttempts , IsLastAttempt , CreatedAt , ConsumerName , PayloadName and TraceId . Use them for idempotency checks and logging. Example [ConsumerTimeout(5)] // Consumer timeouts after 5 seconds [ConsumerAttempts(1)] // Consumer messages moved to poisoned table after 1 failed attempt public class DeleteUsersPosts : IConsumer < UserDeleted > { private readonly ApplicationDbContext _dbContext ; public DeleteUsersPosts ( ApplicationDbContext dbContext ) { _dbContext = dbContext ; } public async Task Consume ( UserDeleted message , ConsumeContext context , CancellationToken cancellationToken ) { ... await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken ); } } Ordering Messages are taken roughly oldest first, but delivery order is not guaranteed : created_at is stored in whole seconds. Messages created in the same second are taken in id order, and ids are random, so their order is effectively arbitrary. A failed message is retried later, after messages that were created after it. Messages in a batch run in parallel by default. [ConsumerExecutionMode(ConsumerExecutionMode.Sequential)] only runs one consumer's messages one at a time within a batch on one processor . It doesn't order them across batches, retries, rails or app instances. Design consumers so the order of messages doesn't matter, for example by checking the current state of the data rather than relying on earlier messages having run. Consumer Failures 💢 Retry Logic : Messages are retried up to MaxAttempts times before they are moved to the poisoned_messages table. Add the [ConsumerAttempts(1)] attribute to override this per consumer. Backoff : The first retry waits AttemptDelay (default 10 seconds), and each later retry waits twice as long as the one before, up to MaxAttemptDelay (default 5 minutes). With the defaults a message is retried after 10, 20, 40 and 80 seconds. Errors : The error from the most recent failed attempt is stored in last_error on both tables, for example System.InvalidOperationException: ... or Timed out after 10 seconds. Interrupted processing : A message is leased while its consumer runs. If the app stops mid-message, the message becomes available again once its consumer timeout plus 30 seconds has passed, and the interrupted attempt counts. Manual Intervention : Use IPoisonedMessageService to count, list, retry or delete poisoned messages. Retrying moves a message back to consumer_messages with its attempts reset. Changes are saved immediately. Retention : Set PoisonedMessageRetention (for example TimeSpan.FromDays(30) ) to delete poisoned messages that old, measured from when they were last due. It runs about once an hour. By default they are kept. Monitoring : Periodically monitor the poisoned_messages table to ensure there are not too many failed messages. public class FailedMessagesController ( IPoisonedMessageService poisoned ) : ControllerBase { [HttpGet] public Task < IReadOnlyList < PoisonedMessageInfo >> List () => poisoned . List ( skip : 0 , take : 50 ); [HttpPost("{id}/retry")] public Task < bool > Retry ( string id ) => poisoned . Retry ( id ); [HttpDelete("{id}")] public Task < bool > Delete ( string id ) => poisoned . Delete ( id ); } Queue statistics 📊 IQueueStatisticsService.Read() returns a snapshot for health checks and dashboards: Available : messages due now and waiting for a processor Waiting : messages not yet due (delayed, waiting to retry, or being processed) OldestAvailableAgeSeconds : how long the longest-waiting due message has been due. If this keeps growing, processors are stuck or falling behind. Poisoned and Schedules : row counts

docs.text: To produce messages in dotnet apps using AsyncMonolith you must first define a consumer payload class. This will act as the body of the message being passed to each consumer configured to handle it. public class OrderCancelled : IConsumerPayload { [JsonPropertyName("order_id")] public string OrderId { get ; set ; } [JsonPropertyName("cancelled_at")] public DateTimeOffset CancelledAt { get ; set ; } } When defining a consumer payload it must derive from the IConsumerPayload interface and be serializable by the System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer . As the consumer payload will be stored in the database in a serialized string, it is a good practice to keep it as small as possible. To produce your message you'll need to inject a IProducerService Immediate messages You can produce messages to be consumed immediately like this: order . Cancel (); _dbContext . Orders . Update ( order ); await _producerService . Produce ( new OrderCancelled () { OrderId = order . Id , CancelledAt = _timeProvider . UtcNow () }); // Save changes await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken ); The message is added to your DbContext and written when you call SaveChangesAsync , in the same transaction as your other changes. If you never save, or the save fails, no message is written. This works the same with every database. Learn more about the Transactional Outbox pattern. Delayed messages You can produce messages to be consumed after a delay by passing a TimeSpan , or at a set time by passing a DateTimeOffset . Times are stored in whole seconds and rounded up, so a message is never consumed early. order . Cancel (); _dbContext . Orders . Update ( order ); await _producerService . Produce ( new OrderCancelled () { OrderId = order . Id , CancelledAt = _timeProvider . UtcNow () }, TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 60 )); // Save changes await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken ); Deduplicated messages Deduplicated messages are useful when you may emit the same message multiple times but only require it to be processed once for a given time period. For instance you may want to aggregate page views no more frequently then once every 10 seconds, you could schedule a reccuring message for this, but it may be wasteful if you anticipate pages go without views for extended periods of time. pageView . Increment (); _dbContext . PageViews . Update ( pageView ); await _producerService . Produce ( new PageViewed () { PageId = pageView . Id , }, TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 10 ), $"page_id:{pageView.Id}" ); // Save changes await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken ); How deduplication works (the key is stored in the insert_id column): While pending only. If a consumer already has a pending message with this deduplication key (saved, or produced on the same DbContext and not yet saved), that consumer is skipped. Once its message has been consumed or poisoned, the same key is accepted again. It is not a permanent idempotency key. Per consumer. For a payload with several consumers, only the consumers that already have the key pending are skipped. Concurrent producers. Two requests producing the same deduplication key at the same moment, in separate transactions, can both pass the check. The unique index on (insert_id, consumer_type) then stops the second, and its SaveChangesAsync throws DbUpdateException . Summary Transactional Persistence : Produce messages along with changes to your DbContext before calling SaveChangesAsync , ensuring your domain changes and the messages they produce are persisted transactionally. Nothing is written until you save. Delay : Pass a TimeSpan delay or a DateTimeOffset to control when a message is consumed. Deduplication : By passing a deduplicationKey , a consumer that already has a pending message with that key is skipped. It is stored in the insert_id column. This is useful when you need a process to take place an amount of time after the first action in a sequence occurred.

docs.text: Frequency : Scheduled messages are produced each time their cron expression occurs, in their time zone. Transactional Persistence : Schedule messages along with changes to your DbContext before calling SaveChangesAsync , ensuring your domain changes and the messages they produce are persisted transactionally. Processing : When a schedule is due, a message is produced for each consumer of its payload and the schedule moves to its next occurrence. Each due schedule is handled on its own, so one that fails doesn't affect the others. To produce your message you'll need to inject a IScheduleService // Publish 'CacheRefreshScheduled' every Monday at 12pm (UTC) with a tag that can be used to modify / delete related scheduled messages. _scheduleService . Schedule ( new CacheRefreshScheduled { Id = id }, "0 0 12 * * MON" , "UTC" , "id:{id}" ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync ( cancellationToken ); Cron expressions Expressions can have 5 fields ( minute hour day month weekday , for example 0 9 * * * for 09:00 daily) or 6 fields with seconds first ( 30 0 9 * * * for 09:00:30). They are evaluated in the time zone you pass, using an IANA id such as Europe/London or UTC . Registering schedules at startup Schedule always inserts a new schedule, so calling it at every startup creates duplicates. Use EnsureSchedule with a tag instead. It creates the schedule the first time, and afterwards updates the payload. It only recalculates the next occurrence if the expression or timezone changed, and removes any duplicates with the same tag. await scheduleService . EnsureSchedule ( new CleanupExpiredSessions (), "0 0 3 * * *" , "Europe/London" , tag : "cleanup-sessions" ); await dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); Occurrences missed while the app was not running are not caught up: the schedule fires once and moves to its next occurrence.

docs.text: Idempotency refers to the ability of an operation to be performed multiple times whilst still yielding the same outcome. It is a critical property of handlers in an event driven system, since events can be reprocessed due to retries, network issues, or other failures. Without idempotency, reprocessing the same event could lead to inconsistent states, duplicate entries, or other unintended side effects. Let's consider a simple scenario where an event handler updates the status of an order. order . Status = "cancelled" ; await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); await _emailService . SendCancellationEmail ( order . Id ); The issue with the above code is that if the event is processed twice the EmailService will send a duplicate email. We can achieve idempotency easily in this scenario by returning early if the order has already been cancelled. if ( order . Status == "cancelled" ){ return ; } order . Status = "cancelled" ; await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); await _emailService . SendCancellationEmail ( order . Id ); You may notice an additional issue with the above example. If the EmailService throws an exception, the message will be retried but will exit early since the Status has already been set to cancelled . This problem can be solved by using AsyncMonolith to emit an OrderCancelled event transactionally along with the changes to your domain, which subsequently invokes a handler that sends an email. Check out the post on the Transactional Outbox pattern to learn more. The revised version using AsyncMonolith may look like this: if ( order . Status == "cancelled" ){ return ; } order . Status = "cancelled" ; await _producerService . Produce ( new OrderCancelled () { OrderId = order . Id }); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); public class SendOrderCancelledEmail : IConsumer < OrderCancelled > { public Task Consume ( OrderCancelled message , ConsumeContext context , CancellationToken cancellationToken ) { ... // Send order cancelled email } } By ensuring that your handlers are idempotent, you can safely reprocess events whilst making sure your system remains consistent and reliable.
docs.title: What is Idempotency?

docs.text: Let's consider a scenario where you are developing an ordering system. When a user cancels an order, you need to cancel the associated shipment and send the user an email confirming the cancellation. order . Cancel (); _dbContext . Orders . Update ( order ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); _shipmentService . CancelShipment ( order . ShipmentId ); _emailService . SendCancellationEmail ( order . Id ); The problem with this approach is that each service is tightly coupled with its dependencies. The OrderService must know to tell ShipmentService and the EmailService that an order has been cancelled. In a simple system, this might not cause significant problems, but as it grows, the number of connections between classes can make them difficult to maintain. The Mediator pattern aims to solve this problem by introducing a Mediator service which acts as a coordinator between services. Each service sends requests to the Mediator without needing to concern itself with the responsibilities of other services. After refactoring the OrderService , it now simply updates the order domain object and tells the Mediator that an order has been canceled: order . Cancel (); _dbContext . Orders . Update ( order ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); _mediator . Send ( new OrderCancelled ( order . Id )); It's the Mediator's job to route the request to each handler configured to handle the OrderCancelled event within their own context. For example the handlers in this scenario could be implemented like this: public class CancelShipmentHandler { public async Task Handle ( OrderCancelled orderCancelled ) { ... shipment . Cancel (); _dbContext . Shipments . Update ( shipment ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); } } public class CancellationEmailHandler { public async Task Handle ( OrderCancelled orderCancelled ) { ... // Send order cancelled email } } This pattern promotes: Code reuse You may have multiple places where an order can be canceled. Now, you don't have to duplicate the logic to cancel the shipment, send an email, or coordinate those actions when an order is cancelled. Single responsibility principle Each handler is responsible for handling the OrderCancelled event within its own context. Open/closed principle Additional handlers can be easily added to extend the behavior of your system without modifying existing code. Testability Handlers can be unit tested in isolation. One issue with the mediator pattern is that a part of your system could fail without recourse. For instance, if the CancelShipmentHandler fails, your system could be left in an inconsistent state since the order has been canceled, the email has been sent but shipment will still be made. AsyncMonolith acts as a mediator, providing the benefits of decoupling while ensuring transactional consistency by using the Transactional Outbox pattern. This ensures that each message is stored in your database before being handled, so if anything fails, it will be retried multiple times before being moved into a poisoned_messages table where you can manually intervene. Refactoring the above scenario to use AsyncMonolith may look like this: order . Cancel (); _dbContext . Orders . Update ( order ); await _producerService . Produce ( new OrderCancelled () { OrderId = order . Id }); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); public class CancelShipment : IConsumer < OrderCancelled > { public Task Consume ( OrderCancelled message , ConsumeContext context , CancellationToken cancellationToken ) { ... shipment . Cancel (); _dbContext . Shipments . Update ( shipment ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); } } public class SendOrderCancelledEmail : IConsumer < OrderCancelled > { public Task Consume ( OrderCancelled message , ConsumeContext context , CancellationToken cancellationToken ) { ... // Send order cancelled email } }

docs.text: Consider a scenario where when a user places an order, you also need to create an entity that tracks the shipment. This scenario is fine as the order and shipment are both committed to your database transactionally; either both succeed, or neither do. You will never have an order created without a shipment. _dbContext . Orders . Add ( newOrder ); _dbContext . Shipments . Add ( newShipment ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); As your application grows, you find that an increasing number of things need to happen when an order is created, and some of them have their own chain of operations. This will quickly cause any method that needs to create an order to grow in complexity and scope. As a result you decide you want to decouple the process of creating an order from the process of creating a shipment, so you adopt an event-driven approach. However, now you have to make a difficult decision: should I commit my order to my database first, then produce an event, or should I produce the event first, then commit the order to my database? In the first scenario, it is possible an order is created but publishing the 'OrderCreated' event fails. // Create order _dbContext . Orders . Add ( newOrder ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); // Dispatch event channel . BasicPublish (...); \\ This fails In the second scenario, it is possible that an event is published, but the order fails to be created. // Dispatch event channel . BasicPublish (...); // Create order _dbContext . Orders . Add ( newOrder ); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); \\ This fails The transactional outbox is a pattern which solves this problem. The general idea is that instead of publishing an event along with making a change to your database, you create an entity that will publish an event at a later time and commit both changes to the database as part of the same transaction. You then have a process capable of checking for records in the outbox table and publishing them as events while handling failures and retries. // Create order _dbContext . Orders . Add ( newOrder ); // Insert event into outbox _dbContext . Outbox . Add ( orderCreated ) await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); For simple use cases, you may realize that the outbox message can act as the event, and you don't actually need the additional step of publishing to a message broker. Instead, you write your events to your database along with the changes to your domain and have a process that periodically fetches, processes, and then removes messages from the outbox table. This is one of the core principles behind AsyncMonolith . In summary, the transactional outbox pattern ensures that events are reliably published, maintaining consistency between operations. While it introduces the need for an additional process to handle the outbox and increases the load on your application database, the benefits of decoupling and reliability often outweigh these overheads. Here is how the above example may look if you’re using AsyncMonolith // Create order _dbContext . Orders . Add ( newOrder ); // Insert event into outbox await _producerService . Produce ( new OrderCreated () { OrderId = order . Id }); await _dbContext . SaveChangesAsync (); public class CreateShipment : IConsumer < OrderCreated > { public Task Consume ( OrderCreated message , ConsumeContext context , CancellationToken cancellationToken ) { ... // Create Order } }
